newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Indonesia, Thailand tops for fixed income - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia, Thailand tops for fixed income - Merrill.

text.p: Fixed income investors will find Indonesia and Thailand worth considering in 1997 in the wake of domestic monetary policy changes and global economic stability, Merrill Lynch said on Tuesday.

William Belchere, head of currency and fixed income analysis and forecasting for Asia, said he saw a continuing rally in the U.S. dollar, with the greenback moving up to 120 yen and 1.7 deutschemark levels over the course of 1997.
U.S. short-term interest rates were "rather stable", as was the global rate environment, Belchere said at a presentation of Merrill Lynch's outlook for the Asia-Pacific region.
Belchere said he expected Indonesia's central bank to widen the rupiah/dollar band on which it bases its interventions to 12-15 percent from the current eight percent.
He also said the Thai central bank was likely to alter its currency basket in the latter half of the year to improve the effectiveness of its monetary policy.
"This is part of a structural change and is an explicit moving away from an exchange rate target," he said.
Belchere said his top three currency trades in the coming year were the rupiah, the baht and the won/yen cross.
"You want to be as long rupiah as you can," he said.
Belchere also said he saw the Indian rupee depreciating by at least six percent.
The top picks in local-currency fixed income markets were Indonesia and Thailand, where interest rates are expected to fall amidst the stable international economic environment, he said.
The offshore market would continue to be dominated by Euro and Yankee issues, he said, adding that a medium- to long-term strategy was advisable with only selective short-term plays.
There would be an increasing presence of Japanese investors in high-yielding bonds as interest rates stay low in Japan, he predicted.
Malaysia and South Korea were likely to see their sovereign ratings upgraded over the course of the year, Belchere said, while Vietnam and Sri Lanka may receive ratings.

The convergence of international economies, in which regional markets quickly feel the impact of events in Europe, the United States and Japan, were among the elements shaping investment decisions, he said.

"Events that happen in the world are transmitted very quickly," Belchere said. Other important trends included financial reforms, the liberalisation of trade through bodies such as the World Trade Organisation, and the "harmonisation of soft infrastructure" such as South Korea's admission to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) last week.
Growth and inflation within the 29-member OECD remained stable, Belchere said.

Politics would also come to the fore in Asia next year as South Korea, Singapore and Pakistan go to the polls and coalition governments face challenges in Thailand and India, he said. -- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6441
